featured_reviews.name: Sneha Dey
featured_reviews.review_text:
TL;DR: A deeply disappointing and distressing experience — sharing this in the interest of women considering her as their OB-GYN, especially during pregnancy.

This is my first-ever negative review for a healthcare provider, and I do not write this lightly.

I am currently 7 months pregnant and visited Dr. Anjali after my routine growth scan on May 15 showed that my AFI was “normal to low” (borderline). My regular gynecologist — a highly reputed senior doctor from Hinduja — was out of town and advised me to consult Dr. Anjali instead of waiting a week.

At no point was I panicking. I was simply following medical advice.

Before visiting, I had a brief phone conversation with Dr. Anjali and shared my report with her on WhatsApp. Despite the report not indicating an emergency, she insisted I come to her clinic that very evening instead of the next day.

I complied.

During the consultation, all my vitals were normal. As part of sharing my pregnancy history, I methodically showed her all my ultrasounds from the last 7 months — around 10 in total — including scans that were medically advised due to:

- a hematoma/bleeding episode,
- reduced fetal movement,
- and a fetal echo concern.

I also mentioned — very matter-of-factly — that my baby was measuring around the 10th percentile. This was shared purely as history, not from a place of anxiety or distress.

What followed was nearly 40 minutes of what felt less like a medical consultation and more like unsolicited psychological evaluation.

Dr. Anjali repeatedly interpreted my medical history as evidence of “panic” and “mental distress,” implying:

- that the number of ultrasounds reflected my anxiety,
- and that mentioning my baby’s percentile reflected my “ignorance” about genetics.

I was stunned.

At no point did she ask for context behind the scans or attempt to understand why they had been medically recommended. Instead, she seemed to reduce valid medical history into a narrative about an “overanxious mother.”

She then shifted into giving extended commentary on maternal mental health and how a mother’s mindset affects the fetus. While that may generally be true, I found it deeply inappropriate that she casually arrived at conclusions about my mental state without basis, context, or qualification.

The most disturbing moment came when she asked whether I take protein powder regularly. I honestly replied that there are days I skip it because it causes nausea and constipation.

To this, she jokingly suggested to my husband that he should give me a “laafa” (slap) because I was “behaving like a child.”

I want to repeat this clearly:
A practicing gynecologist — and someone who claims to counsel women emotionally — suggested physical violence, even if “as a joke,” during a pregnancy consultation.

It was not funny.

Pregnancy is already physically and emotionally demanding. Women constantly navigate fear, societal pressure, medical uncertainty, and vulnerability. The last thing a patient needs is to feel mocked, patronized, psychologically analysed without consent, or shamed for responsibly sharing medical history.

What saddened me most was not just the lack of empathy, but the normalization of such behaviour by another woman doctor.

Patients deserve:

- respect,
- informed medical guidance,
- emotional safety,
- and the freedom to ask questions or share concerns without being trivialized.

A consultation should never leave a pregnant woman feeling humiliated, dismissed, or emotionally exhausted.

Dr. Anjali, if you are reading this: empathy is not optional in healthcare. And if mental health is something you wish to advise patients on, perhaps begin with understanding boundaries, sensitivity, and dignity.

If not, please stick to obstetrics.

featured_reviews.name: Sil Fun
featured_reviews.review_text:
Very important pro tip when ordering food from the canteen on the ground floor of this hospital:

If you have permission to eat on the upper floors where medical tests are conducted, because your family member cannot come down to the ground floor, do not tell any canteen staff that you are taking the food upstairs. Also, if you order a large amount of food, act as if your family member is sitting somewhere on the ground floor.

The reason is that the person who hands out food trays may refuse to give you a tray. In my experience, he created unnecessary problems for me.

After ordering more than ₹500 worth of food, he insisted that I eat the patties first and then the pizza and pasta later. I told him to give me everything at once. I also honestly informed him that my brother was upstairs as a patient undergoing tests and that we had permission to eat there.

I assumed he was trying to help, but after making me wait 20–30 minutes, when it was finally time to collect my order, he told me that trays were not allowed on the upper floors. He could have told me this before taking the order, but he didn't. It felt as though he waited until the food was ready because he thought I might cancel the order otherwise.

What's the point of allowing food to be taken upstairs if trays are not allowed? It seemed like an unnecessary rule that only created problems.

I eventually took the food upstairs without a tray. It was difficult because the plates were much smaller. My brother, who could barely walk properly, and I tried our best not to drop any food on the floor. However, crumbs from the patties and corn from the pizza still fell because the plates were too small for carrying so much food.

Hinduja Hospital, we visited your hospital for tests for my brother that cost around ₹10,000. Everyone on the upper floors—including the doctors, nurses, and reception staff—was professional, friendly, and helpful.

However, I am giving this review 1 star.

I am 29 years old, and this is the first time in my life that I have given anyone a 1-star review. Unfortunately, your canteen employee on the ground floor—the person handling payments, food distribution, and trays—left such a poor impression that it overshadowed an otherwise positive experience.

This incident happened in June 2025. I am writing this review a year later because I still remember how I was treated and how frustrating the experience was.

Menopause Is Not the End — It's a New Chapter
Menopause is a natural biological transition, yet for many women, it arrives accompanied by confusion, discomfort, and a concerning lack of reliable medical guidance. At Dr. Tanushree Pandey's clinic in South Mumbai, we believe every woman deserves clear information and supportive care through every stage of her reproductive life — including and beyond menopause.

Menopause is confirmed after 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period, typically between ages 45 and 55. The years leading up to it — perimenopause — can begin as early as the mid-30s, bringing with them a range of symptoms that are often attributed to stress, ageing, or other causes.

Common symptoms of perimenopause and menopause:
• Hot flashes and night sweats
• Irregular or heavy periods (in perimenopause)
• Sleep disturbances
• Mood changes, anxiety, or low mood
• Vaginal dryness and discomfort during intercourse
• Reduced libido
• Urinary frequency or leakage
• Cognitive changes, including difficulty concentrating
• Bone density loss (increasing risk of osteoporosis)

These symptoms are real, and they are treatable. Options range from lifestyle modifications and non-hormonal therapies to Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT), which — when appropriately prescribed — is safe and highly effective for most women.
At Dr. Pandey's clinic, menopause care is individualised, evidence-based, and delivered with the sensitivity this important life stage deserves.

Cervical Cancer Awareness: Prevention Saves Lives
Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers — and yet it remains the second most common cancer among women in India. The reason this statistic persists is not lack of treatment; it is lack of awareness and access to screening.

Cervical cancer is caused almost entirely by persistent infection with high-risk strains of the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — a common virus transmitted through sexual contact. Critically, HPV infection often causes no symptoms at all, which is why regular screening is so essential.

What every woman should know:

PAP Smear: A cervical screening test that detects abnormal cells before they become cancerous. Recommended every 3 years from age 21, or every 5 years with combined HPV testing from age 30.

HPV Vaccination: Highly effective vaccines are available that protect against the most common cancer-causing HPV strains. Ideally given before sexual debut, but beneficial up to age 45 in many cases. Vaccination + screening together provide the strongest protection.

Warning signs to never ignore: unusual vaginal discharge (watery, foul-smelling, or blood-tinged), bleeding between periods or after intercourse, pelvic pain, and pain during intercourse.

When detected early, cervical cancer is highly treatable. When detected late, outcomes are significantly poorer. The difference, in most cases, is a simple, painless screening test.

Endometriosis: The Condition That Takes Too Long to Diagnose
Endometriosis affects approximately 10% of women of reproductive age worldwide — yet on average, it takes 7 to 10 years to receive a correct diagnosis. This delay is not just frustrating — it allows the condition to progress, causing increasing pain, damage to reproductive organs, and reduced fertility potential.

So what is endometriosis? It is a condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus — on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, bladder, bowel, and other surrounding structures. Each month, this tissue responds to hormonal changes just as the uterine lining does — swelling, breaking down, and bleeding — but with nowhere to go. This causes inflammation, the formation of scar tissue (adhesions), and often, intense pain.

Key symptoms to watch for:
• Severe menstrual cramps that worsen over time
• Chronic pelvic pain, not just during periods
• Pain during or after sexual intercourse
• Painful bowel movements or urination, especially during menstruation
• Heavy or irregular periods
• Difficulty conceiving

Endometriosis is frequently dismissed as "bad periods" — both by women themselves and sometimes by healthcare providers. If you have experienced any of these symptoms for more than a few cycles, a thorough gynaecological assessment is essential.
